claims.text: The baseline is a W–Ta–Ti–V–Cr refractory high-entropy alloy produced by elemental powder mixing and spark plasma sintering without targeted secondary-phase control.
Adjusting alloy chemistry and spark-plasma-sintering conditions can produce in-situ TiC precipitates in a W-based refractory HEA.
The processing intervention will yield a controlled volume fraction of TiC nanoprecipitates.
The TiC nanoprecipitates will be uniformly distributed in the alloy matrix.
The TiC nanoprecipitates will form coherent interfaces with the matrix.
The TiC nanoprecipitates will be embedded in a BCC alloy matrix.
TiC interfaces will absorb radiation-induced point defects.
TiC interfaces will promote recombination of radiation-induced point defects.
Point-defect absorption and recombination at TiC interfaces will mitigate helium-bubble nucleation and growth.
Coherent TiC particles will facilitate dislocation transmission.
Dislocation transmission at TiC particles will relieve local stress concentrations.
In-situ TiC will improve the alloy's radiation tolerance.
The TiC-containing alloy will maintain or enhance hardness and strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
The TiC-containing alloy will preserve ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
The intervention is compatible with scalable and practical powder-metallurgy processing.
Under irradiation, the modified alloy will exhibit lower helium-bubble size and density than the unmodified baseline.
Under irradiation, the modified alloy will exhibit greater resistance to irradiation hardening than the unmodified baseline.
The beneficial effects will hold at temperatures of at least 1000 K under high helium or neutron fluxes representative of fusion divertor service.
Departures from the optimum TiC volume fraction, size distribution, or coherence could impair ductility or produce an inhomogeneous radiation response.
